heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background, 1.2 Our work, Figure 1)
note: 15 and 16 are context: 15 defines the higher education system as an organisational structure of institutions plus personnel and infrastructure and asserts that a healthy system 'can bring a lot of value to the country' without a single number; 16 is the gap claim, that researchers evaluate a university's system and rarely the national one, and ends on a collapse warning. 17 routes to an index evaluation model and glues the '1.2 Our work' heading into its tail. 18-20 are the three work paragraphs and they are the paper's own map: 18 states the weighting recipe (AHP + entropy weight + coefficient of variation), TOPSIS as the aggregator, 40 countries, fuzzy clustering into three - actually four - categories; 19 introduces INNI, the exponential fit and the derived indicator NRHHE; 20 states the one-way ANOVA selection of five indicators, the three-phase policy for Italy and the system dynamics evaluation. 21 announces the structure figure and 22 is its caption, whose tail also holds the '2 Assumption and Notation' and '2.1 Assumption' headings, so chapter 2 starts inside a figure caption. Block 14 is the printed "1 Introduction 1.1 Background" heading, measured as its own block; it is glued to the paragraph it heads (group 14-15) so no measured block on page 3 stays uncoded.

heading: 2 Assumption and Notation (2.1 Assumption, 2.2 Notation)
note: 23 frames the four hypotheses. Each hypothesis is split one or two printed lines per block. Assumption 1 (24-25) simply asserts that the five superior indicators exhaust the influences on health - 'resource, environment, connect, achievement and sustainable' - which is the modelling choice dressed as a premise. Assumption 2 (26-27) sets a tolerance: two countries whose INNI differ by less than 0.03 count as the same economic level. That number is load-bearing, because the choice of the UK as Italy's reference country rests on it, and it is never justified. Assumption 3 (28-29) says Italy will adopt the authors' policy, which is what lets 6.3 report a simulated effect as a result. Assumption 4 (30-32) freezes the UK for 15 years 'so its NHHE will not change significantly', which is what makes the 95%-of-UK target well defined. 32's tail carries the '2.2 Notation' heading and the first table row. 33-37 are the whole notation table as one job: NHHE, INNI, NRHHE, F (F-test statistic), the value of the i-th indicator in the j-th year and its standardised form. Five symbols for a paper that runs on R, E, C, A, S, y_ij, p_ij, entropy, weights and TOPSIS distances.

heading: 3 Establish NHHE Evaluation Model (3.1 Indicators, 3.2 Normalization of Inferior Indicators, 3.3 Determination of the Weights, 3.4 Calculate NHHE, 3.5 Determine their health)
note: 38 routes the chapter and defines NHHE as the target quantity. 39-41 define the framework: a healthy system gives teachers and students resources, a good environment, outside connections, achievement and sustainability, so NHHE is a function of R, E, C, A, S (40 names them); 41 fixes the size of the model at 5 superior and 23 inferior indicators and points at the framework figure, 42's caption. 43-44 route to indicator definition; 45-50 define the five groups one block each: R1 expenditure on higher education as % of GDP, R2 R&D expenditure, R3 expenditure per student, R4 social donations, R5 student-teacher ratio; E1 equity index, E2 freedom of higher education policy, E3 national competitiveness contribution; C1 international teachers, C2 international students, C3 international co-authored papers, C4 teacher-industry co-authored papers; A1 employment index, A2 graduate debt ratio, A3 patents per capita, A4 Nobel and Fields winners, A5 total papers, A6 top-1000 universities; S1 enrolment rate, S2 full-time researchers, S3 cost index, S4 promotion rate, S5 salary index. That is 23, and the five group headings (Resource, Environment, Connect, Achievement, Sustainable) are all glued into the tails of the previous block, so they cost no measured block. 51 names five normalisation methods (logistic, maximum, minimum, moderate, subordinate function) but the moderate method is never used or defined again - four appear, five are claimed. 52-63 are the normalisation rules, one derivation each: the logistic function with its three endpoint conditions and the two parameters that are 'determined in the solution of the model' and nowhere reported; maximum normalisation for benefit indicators; minimum normalisation for cost indicators, whose 'optimal value' is written where the maximum belongs; and the partial-large Cauchy membership for discrete grades, calibrated by grade 1 -> 0.01, grade 3 -> 0.8, grade 5 -> 1. 64 is the only account of the outcome - 'all the inferior indicators can be normalized ... we omit the detailed methods for each inferior indicator' - so which of the 23 indicators got which method is never stated. 65 routes to the combination weighting and states the motive, that AHP alone is subjective. 66-69 are the AHP steps: hierarchical structure, judgment matrices (67-68) which are explicitly withheld ('because of the limited space, we will not show the judgment matrix'), and a consistency check (69) whose 'results are shown below' and are never shown. 70-74 are the entropy weight method: probability matrix, information entropy, weight formula. 75-82 are the coefficient of variation method for the five superior factors: CV formula, standard deviation, weight from CV, then the combination step in 81-82, which announces the AHP weight, the EWM weight and the CVM weight and stops before giving the combination formula - the block ends and Figure 3's callout takes over. That is the sharpest gap in the chapter: the whole weighting engine is three formulas plus three withheld inputs, and its output appears only as a figure (83). 84-85 select 40 countries (no list, no criterion beyond 'different continents and different development situations') and run TOPSIS. 86-90 are the TOPSIS steps: optimal and worst scheme, distances, closeness, with the composite score defined implicitly by 'the higher the score, the healthier'. 91-93 report the clustering: four classes (super healthy, healthy, sub-healthy, unhealthy) from a fuzzy cluster analysis whose centroids are not printed, with the figure numbers crossed - 91 introduces 'Figure 4' as the clustering and captions 'Figure 5: Fuzzy clustering / Figure 4: Classification map', then 92 reads 'Figure 5' as the clustering source. The classification standard is Figure 6 (93).

heading: 4.1 Introduction of new indicator: INNI (regression of the 23 indicators on INNI, NRHHE definition)
note: 94 defines the extension: because the health ranking correlates with income, health is assumed to depend both on the system's own indicators and on the level of economic development, so INNI enters. 95 checks that assumption with linear and quadratic regressions of all 23 indicators on INNI and reports that every indicator rises with INNI except A2 (graduate debt ratio) and S3 (cost index) - the two that should fall, which is consistent, though the fit statistics are not given. 96-97 derive the exponential trend equation NHHE = f(INNI) and its fitted coefficients; 98-99 are the lead and caption of Figure 7. 100 defines NRHHE as the vertical position relative to that curve: above the curve is relatively healthy, below is relatively unhealthy. 101 computes the Italian case: 26th of 40 on raw NHHE (0.31) but 40th of 40 once income is accounted for, which is the justification for choosing Italy. 102 defines the equivalence band (INNI within 0.03) that assumption 2 set up, and 103 applies it: Italy's INNI 0.80 gives the band 0.77-0.83. 104 compares within the band, finds the UK, and elects it reference; the block also glues the '4.2 Vision for the next 15 years' and '4.2.1 Forecast the change of INNI' headings into its tail. Note that 104 says 'we make this interval in Figure 6', but Figure 6 is the classification-standard chart; the scatter with the band is Figure 7.

heading: 4.2 Vision for the next 15 years (4.2.1 Forecast the change of INNI, 4.2.2 A comparative analysis of Italy and UK, 4.2.3 Vision development)
note: 105 routes to a fifteen-year horizon and argues only weakly for it ('it is necessary to implement policies over a longer period'). 106-107 compute the INNI series for Italy and the UK from 1995 to 2019 and fit four exponential-smoothing variants (simple non-linear, Holt linear trend, Brown linear trend, damped trend); 108 is Table 1's caption, 109-110 read the fit and pick Holt, whose R-squared is 0.6367 and 0.6393 for the two countries - the coefficients of the chosen model are never printed, only the ranking of the four alternatives. 111 defines the smoothing parameters and 112 captions Figure 8's prediction curve. 113 is the 4.2.2 heading as its own block. 114-116 read the two comparison charts: Italy scores below the UK on all five superior indicators and on 15 of the 23 inferior ones, which is the evidence base for the vision; the figure references slip, since 114 cites 'Figure 8' for the radar charts, which are Figures 9 and 10. 117 computes the UK forecast (INNI 0.81296 to 0.83129 over 15 years) and announces Table 2, 118 is that table read as one block - NHHE 0.44, Resource 0.49853, Environment 0.75650, Connect 0.76877, Achievement 0.28799, Sustainable 0.49862 - and the six numbers do not hang together, because a weighted composite of five sub-scores of which four are between 0.49 and 0.77 cannot be 0.44 unless the weights are concentrated on the 0.29 achievement score, and no weights are given. 119 computes the Italian target as 95% of the UK's NHHE with the reason stated only as 'after taking into account the factors of comprehensive national strength' - the 95% has no derivation - and 120's lone number 0.47369 is the tail of that arithmetic spilling into its own block, with the '4.3' heading after it.

heading: 4.3 Assessment of health status in Italy (Assessment of NHHE, Assessment of NRHHE)
note: 121 routes to two assessments, absolute and relative. 122 substitutes the vision-state data into the NHHE model and 123 captions the comparison chart; 124 interprets: Italy is sub-healthy now and healthy in 15 years, with resource, achievement and sustainable moving sub-healthy to healthy, environment sub-healthy to super healthy, and connect healthy to super healthy. So four of the five factors are predicted to improve at least one class, which is a strong claim for a plan whose mechanism is only evaluated later in chapter 6. 125-127 repeat the exercise for NRHHE and read the point's move from below the curve to above it. The two assessments use the same inputs, so the second adds no independent evidence - it re-expresses the first relative to income.

heading: 5 Presentation of policies (5.1 Extraction of key indicators, 5.2 Formulation of policy, Table 4)
note: 128 routes: 23 indicators are too many to carry a policy, so the model is to be reduced to a few key ones. 129-131 give the correlation coefficient formula and its symbols; 132 checks and reports strong pairwise correlation between many indicators, which motivates the reduction (and, unremarked, weakens the claim that the 23 indicators measure different things). 133-136 derive the one-way ANOVA machinery - variance at each level, inter- and intra-group mean squares, the F statistic - and 137 checks the result: five indicators, R1, E2, C1, A6, S2, have significant effects. They fall one per factor (R1 in Resource, E2 in Environment, C1 in Connect, A6 in Achievement, S2 in Sustainable), which is why the policy package has exactly five sections and why each section's most important lever is not chosen against the others but inside its own factor. The 10% step used for the ANOVA perturbation is stated in 132 and never referenced again. 138 routes the three-phase plan (2021-2035, five years a phase) and 139 is Figure 13's caption with the Resource bullet in its tail. 140-144 are the five policy paragraphs, one per factor, labelled Resource, Environment, Connect, Achievement, Sustainable, with each label glued into the previous paragraph's tail; they are long prescriptive blocks (152, 193, 143, 100, 138 words) of institutional advice - competitive allocation, university governance reform, talent policy, first-class disciplines, teacher development - and they contain no Italian number beyond the earlier 1.5% of GDP. 145 announces the schedule and starts Table 4, and 146-159 are the fifteen table rows read as one job: three stages per factor, each stage one instrument. The table is the paper's actual policy product, and it is where the plan's resolution stops: the instruments are named but none is quantified, so the system dynamics model of chapter 6 has to supply the magnitudes itself.

heading: 6 Evaluation of the effectiveness of policies (6.1 design, 6.2 transmission, 6.3 implementation, 6.4 feedback)
note: 160-161 route to a four-aspect evaluation (design, transmission, implementation, feedback) and the chapter then evaluates itself one aspect at a time. 6.1 is pure claim: 162-163 argue multi-objective design reaches the optimum because it considers five aspects at once; 164-165 argue targeting works because Italy's situation was studied; 166-167 argue continuity works because the plan is in three five-year stages. None of the three is tested - they are properties of the design asserted as results. 168-170 are the transmission part and the only model in the chapter: a system dynamics flow graph, described unit by unit in 169 (red hexagon objective, pink rectangles the five intervention policies, red arrows implementation, green and blue arrows the couplings between inferior indicators) and captioned in 170. The graph's couplings are never given as equations or coefficients, so 6.3's numbers come from a model whose structure is a picture. 171 claims the incentive and competition mechanisms mobilise implementers. 172 computes the implementation case: Italian higher education spending is 1.5% of GDP now and assumed to reach 2% under the plan, and that annual figure is fed in as the policy input; 173 interprets the simulated NHHE path as accelerating growth, which is read as proof of effectiveness. The 1.5% -> 2% move is an assumption, not a policy from chapter 5, and it is the only quantitative intervention in the paper. 174-175 describe the feedback loop: bad feedback in one period is corrected in the next, so the three-step plan is adaptive. That is a mechanism claim with no feedback rule, no measurement and no iteration.

heading: 7 The impact of our plan on Italy (7.1 students, 7.2 faculty, 7.3 schools, 7.4 communities, 7.5 nation)
note: Five stakeholder sections, each with a benefits paragraph and a risks paragraph, and the pair is the honest part of the paper: every benefit is followed by a cost. Students: tuition down and enrolment up, against the funding risk, the long payback of research investment and the pandemic shock named explicitly ('under the influence of novel coronavirus pneumonia, the national economy has been greatly impacted'). Faculty: development projects raise teaching quality, against the resource cost, the coercion effect and the fact that training is evaluated by the trainers. Schools: performance-based funding rewards reform, against polarisation between strong and weak schools and the cosmetic merging of disciplines. Communities: graduates relieve labour shortages, against residents' narrow view and missing facilities. Nation: talent inflows and citizen quality, against the funding ceiling and the equity cost of rising tuition. 183-184 is one paragraph split at the page break. 188 closes with the summary judgment - conditions are 'insufficient and unstable', resources wasted, efficiency low, funds short - and glues the '8 Sensitivity Analysis' heading into its tail. The chapter is interpretable as a mechanism/limit alternation because the two kinds of block make opposite claims about the same instrument; that alternation is the paper's only systematic treatment of risk.

heading: 8 Sensitivity Analysis
note: One perturbation, one figure, one conclusion. 189 takes the system dynamics model, moves Italy's higher education investment by +0.5% and -0.5% of GDP and re-runs; 190 captions Figure 16; 191 interprets the trend as unchanged with a deviation 'within an acceptable range', so the model is called stable. What is tested is the effect of the policy input, not the model's parameters: the weights, the 80% bands, the 0.03 INNI tolerance, the 95% target and the clustering thresholds are all held fixed, so the sensitivity analysis says the projection is monotone in spending, which it is by construction.

heading: 9 Strengths and Weaknesses
note: 191's tail carries the '9 Strengths and Weaknesses' heading and the first bullet label, so the chapter opens inside the previous block. Three strengths: two models, one ignoring and one including economic development, which is called 'more objective and accurate'; a vision anchored on the UK rather than guessed; a four-aspect policy evaluation made quantitative by system dynamics. The first claim is weak in the direction that matters, since the second model is the first plus a fitted curve, so its accuracy is inherited. Two weaknesses, and both are real: indicator selection is subjective and the classification of some indicators is vague; and the pre-period health of Italy and the UK was never computed, only forecast from INNI, so the baseline is a prediction. 196 hands the '10 Conclusion' heading into its tail.

heading: 10 Conclusion
note: 197 restates the NHHE model and the four classes. 198-199 restate the two-model comparison of Italy and the UK and conclude that Italy's health improves substantially in the vision state - one paragraph split at the page break. 200 restates the ANOVA selection of five indicators, the five-year plan, the system dynamics evaluation and the impact analysis, ends on the admission that change is difficult, and glues the 'Reference' heading into its tail. References run 201-203 (16 items, no in-text citation numbers anywhere in the body except the two arXiv-style entries, so the reference list is unattached to the argument). Nothing in the conclusion reports an uncertainty on any of the numbers, and the 2035 target date of the summary sheet appears in the body only through the three-phase schedule of 138.
